title: Accelerating Benchmarking via Structure-aware Core-set Selection
one_liner: Pick a tiny representative slice of brain imaging data that lets you rank models accurately without testing them all.
lead: Scientists need to test many brain imaging analysis methods on huge datasets, but that takes too long. This paper does something smarter: it picks a small, carefully chosen subset of the data that ranks the methods the same way as using all the data. The key is to find samples where brain structure is stable during learning, and to spread those samples across different types of brain patterns.

problem.h2: Why testing hundreds of methods takes forever
paras: Brain scientists use brain imaging scans (fMRI) to map how brain regions talk to each other. To understand which mapping method works best, they need to test dozens or hundreds of methods on huge datasets. Testing one method on one dataset takes an hour. Testing 200 methods takes 200 hours.

A naive first try: test every method on the whole dataset. That works, but it is so slow that scientists never do it in practice — so they never really know which methods are best. The bottleneck is that there are so many method-dataset combinations (the paper calls this the combinatorial explosion).

callout.html: Pick 10% of the data (a core-set) that ranks methods the same way as 100% of the data, so you get accurate rankings in one tenth the time.

panels.title: 1. The problem
panels.caption: Thousands of brain scans, hundreds of methods. Testing all is too slow.

panels.title: 2. Old approach: random subset
panels.caption: Picking random scans misranks methods. Method A looks best but actually is not.

panels.title: 3. The paper's move: measure structure stability
panels.caption: Scans where brain structure stays stable during learning get high stability scores.

panels.title: 4. Spread across brain patterns
panels.caption: Combine stable scans with spreading across different brain pattern types.

panels.title: 5. Result: tiny core-set ranks methods correctly
panels.caption: 10% of data ranks methods as accurately as 100%, 10x faster.

steps.text: A transformer (a machine learning model) reads each scan's brain structure and learns how each region connects to others.
Measure how much the learned brain pattern shifts during training. Stable scans get high scores; noisy ones get low scores.
Sort all scans by their stability score and keep only the top 10%, which represent foundational brain patterns.
Within the stable samples, add a spreading step (kernel density estimation) so the core-set covers different brain pattern clusters.
Rank all methods using only this tiny core-set. The ranking matches the ranking from the full dataset.

paras: The paper changes which scans you pick. Instead of randomly selecting scans or picking based on how a single method trains on them, it selects based on structural stability — how reliably the learned brain patterns hold up during training.

hidden.h2: Structural Perturbation Score: the stability measure
hidden.name: Structural Perturbation Score
paras: The hidden quantity is the Structural Perturbation Score (SPS). It measures how much a brain scan's learned structure (the connectivity pattern) shifts from one training epoch (round) to the next. Think of it like watching a photograph: if the same scene photographed twice looks almost identical, the stability is high. If small details jump around a lot, stability is low.

The paper estimates SPS by taking the learned brain pattern at each training epoch, comparing it to the pattern from the previous epoch, and measuring the difference. Scans with low differences (stable patterns) are the ones selected for the core-set.

heat.caption: Darker means higher stability score. Top scans (darkest, marked) selected for core-set.

reads.html: The Structural Perturbation Score asks: when the model learns from this scan, how much does its understanding of the brain structure jump around? Stable scans are trustworthy representatives of brain patterns.

SPS measures the Frobenius norm (the length of a multidimensional difference, a list of numbers) between the learned structure matrix at epoch e and epoch e-1, summed over all training epochs. The formula shows: take each epoch's learned pattern, subtract the previous epoch's pattern, measure how long that difference is, square it, and average across all epochs.

mechanism.h2: Why ranking is preserved when you pick stable scans
paras: The core insight is that noisy, unstable scans throw off method rankings. When a method trains on a scan where the learned brain structure bounces around, the method's final performance is partly luck (which random noise hit during training) instead of whether the method is fundamentally good. Stable scans filter out that noise.

Here is the causal chain: (1) Each brain imaging method learns by comparing its guess of brain structure to the real data. (2) If the data is noisy, a weak method can accidentally guess right once, or get fooled by random patterns. (3) If you pick scans where the learned structure is rock-solid during training, you get a fair test — the method either actually understands the brain pattern or it does not. (4) This fairness is preserved: the methods' relative ranking on stable scans matches their ranking on all scans. Adding the diversity step ensures you are not just picking a single type of stable brain pattern — you cover all the archetypes.

math.words: The Structural Perturbation Score (SPS) is the average difference between learned brain structures at consecutive training rounds.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scan A: learned structures at epochs differ by 0.2, 0.1, 0.3, 0.1 per epoch. Sum = 0.7. Average = 0.7 / 4 = 0.175.
Scan B: learned structures at epochs differ by 2.0, 1.8, 2.1, 1.9 per epoch. Sum = 7.8. Average = 7.8 / 4 = 1.95.
Scan A (SPS=0.175) is stable, selected. Scan B (SPS=1.95) is noisy, skipped. Methods tested on Scan A ranking are more reliable.

math.note: Lower SPS means the learned brain patterns are stable, so the core-set selects low-SPS scans as representatives.

bars.h2: How well does ranking survive on the core-set?

charts.title: Random core-set (baseline)
charts.note: Random scans flip the rankings. Method A drops from best to 5th place.

charts.title: SCLCS core-set (this paper)
charts.note: Stable, diverse scans preserve rankings. Methods that are best on all data are still best on core-set.

items.b: Core-set is too small to span brain pattern diversity.
items.html: If you only keep the top 5% most stable scans, you might miss rare but important brain patterns. Solution: use the density-aware sampling step to force spreading.

items.b: Stability during training does not mean good for ranking.
items.html: A scan might be stable but not representative of the real variety in brains. Solution: the contrastive learning step (training the model with a loss that rewards learning similar patterns from similar scans) ensures stable scans are truly representative.

items.b: Method designed for single-model benchmarking fails here.
items.html: Old core-set methods optimize for helping one model train faster by minimizing the single model's error. Ranking many methods fairly is different — you need samples where all methods shine or struggle together, so their differences are clear. A sample that speeds up method A might hide method B's true strength, because optimizing for one model's loss steers toward different samples than optimizing for multi-method ranking consistency.

Combining structural stability (SPS) with diversity sampling ensures the core-set is both rock-solid (methods trained on it learn clearly) and representative (it covers all major brain pattern types).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment on publicly available brain imaging data: (1) Take a real fMRI dataset with at least 50 samples and 5 different brain connectivity methods. (2) Compute method rankings on the full dataset (ground truth). (3) Apply SCLCS to select a 10% core-set. (4) Compute method rankings on only the core-set. (5) Measure how well the core-set ranking matches the full ranking using a rank correlation metric (the paper uses nDCG@k, which scores how many of the top-k methods are ranked the same).
demo.metric_eq: nDCG@k = (gain from correctly ranked methods at position k) / (ideal ranking gain)
demo.closing: The demo is successful if the core-set (10% of data) ranks the methods with at least 90 percent consistency with the full-data ranking. The paper shows 23 percent improvement over baselines in this metric.
